Securitize to Acquire River One, Expanding Into $6 Trillion Asset-Backed Finance Market

Tokenization platform Securitize (NYSE: $SECZ) agreed Monday to acquire River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform built around the stablecoin economy, as it expands into a private asset-backed finance market estimated at more than $6 trillion.

The acquisition, announced alongside Securitize's third-quarter financial results, would expand its tokenization infrastructure into warehouse financing, allowing institutions to borrow against pools of loans and other assets before selling, refinancing or otherwise distributing them. The deal also represents the first major deployment of the roughly $400 million CEO Carlos Domingo told said in July the company planned to allocate toward acquisitions following its public listing.

According to Securitize's earnings announcement, River One was incubated by Framework Ventures and backed by Framework and Maple Finance. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to customary closing conditions. Financial terms were not disclosed.

Domingo described credit as "one of the most exciting emerging asset classes" for blockchain-based financial markets. The private asset-backed finance market was valued at approximately $6.1 trillion in 2024 and is projected to exceed $9 trillion by 2029, according to a KKR report cited by CoinDesk.

Securitize also reported third-quarter revenue of $18.6 million, up 13% from $16.5 million a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Tokenization revenue climbed 28% to $11.5 million, while asset servicing revenue declined 6% to $7.2 million. Average tokenized assets on the platform reached a record $5.0 billion, an increase of 39%, with $4.8 billion in assets on the platform as of Sept. 30. Transaction volume increased 20% to $4.3 billion. Meanwhile, assets under administration in its fund services business fell 29% to $25.2 billion.

The company reported a net loss of $66.3 million, or $0.41 per diluted share, compared with net income of $4.1 million in the same quarter last year. Approximately $60 million, or roughly 90% of the reported loss, stemmed from largely non-cash expenses and accounting charges associated with its business combination and public listing. These included a $23.2 million change in the fair value of earnout liabilities and a $20.6 million loss related to the settlement of convertible instruments.

Bill Gates' Microsoft Copilot AI predicts an astonishing price target for Solana (SOL USD price) by January 1, 2027, estimating it to reach between $1,000 and $2,000, with a potential stretch target exceeding $2,500. This outlook assumes the return of a robust cryptocurrency bull market, fueled by a hypothetical groundbreaking event.

As of November 9, 2026, SOL is trading near $87, meaning the Copilot prediction would require nearly a 25x return to reach its stretch target of $2,500. This prediction is intentionally extreme and far beyond typical forecasts.

(SOURCE: Bill Gates Copilot AI Predicts Historic SOL Crypto Price)

Copilot AI anticipates a strong bull market in late 2026, driven by a major global consortium adopting Solana as the primary high-throughput blockchain for consumer applications and real-time payments.

The hypothetical catalyst is SOL becoming integrated into everyday on-chain activities; demand for Solana is expected to surge as both a utility token and a speculative asset.

Bill Gates Microsoft Copilot Predicts a Wild Solana Price Target: What Does the Technical Analysis Say?

On the higher timeframes, Solana has been consolidating in the $70–$75 region after reclaiming key levels from earlier lows. Price is holding above important intermediate moving averages following its rebound.

In a standard bull market, a sustained break above $100–$120 would open the path toward the prior all-time high near $296. Under the extreme mass-adoption scenario outlined above, clearing that previous high would likely trigger powerful measured-move extensions and multi-cycle Fibonacci projections from the long-term base.

This is what would theoretically support a move into the $1,000–$2,000+ zone if volume and institutional/consumer flows expand dramatically. RSI currently sits in neutral-to-constructive territory with significant room to run into the extreme overbought levels typical of parabolic advances.

Key nearer-term supports sit in the $110–$115 and $100–$105 zones; holding those would keep the broader recovery structure intact while the market prices in any major narrative shifts.

Overall, while the current chart supports continued upside in a normal bull market, only an extraordinary surge in real-world, high-throughput adoption could justify the multi-thousand-percent extension implied by the $1,000–$2,500 targets.

Key Takeaways

IREN stock is down 72% from its peak a year ago, and Cantor Fitzgerald cut its price target to $47 from $99 on Nov. 6 while keeping an Overweight rating.

IREN moved its target for more than $4 billion of annualized revenue to January, and possibly February, after Microsoft asked for a design change and suppliers ran late.

Analysts expect revenue to nearly quadruple to $2.8 billion in fiscal 2027, but their loss estimate for that year has widened to $3.42 a share from $0.94 three months ago.

Cantor's $47 works out to 6.6x forward sales, above IREN's 3-year average of 5.2x. With losses widening and $6 billion of the build still to be funded, it looks more like a two-year target than a one-year one.

IREN (IREN:NASDAQ) has lost 72% since its peak a year ago, and Cantor Fitzgerald still sees it more than doubling.

On Nov. 6, Cantor analyst Brett Knoblauch cut his price target to $47 from $99 and kept an Overweight rating. That's 117% above the Nov. 6 close of $21.64, even after the stock jumped 20.02% that day on its first-quarter report.

Microsoft asked for a change, and the date moved

On Nov. 4, The Information reported, citing unnamed sources, that Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) pushed back AI spending in the September quarter because of delays at IREN's Childress, Texas site.

IREN's first-quarter report the next day confirmed the slip. "The more than $4 billion of contracted ARR is funded and now targeted for January, after a customer-requested design change and supplier timing moved it from year-end; it may extend to the end of February," co-CEO Daniel Roberts said in the release. On the call, he named Microsoft as the customer that asked for the change.

Cantor trimmed, but stayed bullish

Cantor cut its calendar 2028 adjusted EBITDA estimates and the multiple it puts on them.

title: The Stock Market Is “Petrified of Oracle’s Balance Sheet” as Microsoft Walks Away

The Stock Market Is "Petrified of Oracle's Balance Sheet" as Microsoft Walks Away ©@yhelfman via Canva, @Yurich84 from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Microsoft is winding down a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle, days after Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip-leasing deal with Tencent.

The Microsoft contract itself looks small, but losing it leaves Oracle's backlog leaning even harder on OpenAI, which S&P says accounts for about half of it.

Oracle's free cash flow was negative $23.7 billion in fiscal 2026, its total debt reached $167 billion, and it sold another $20 billion of stock and notes on Nov. 2.

The market's fear looks justified until Oracle's mid-December results show its backlog growing with customers other than OpenAI.

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) has stopped renewing a deal to rent AI computing power from Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) and is winding it down, Bloomberg reported on Friday. It's part of a wider review of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships.

That makes two AI deals Oracle has lost in a week. On Wednesday, Oracle canceled an estimated $7 billion chip-leasing deal with Tencent after pressure from the Trump administration, the Financial Times reported.

Investors were already nervous about the stock before either deal fell through. On Friday's weekly wrap of The Real Eisman Playbook, Steve Eisman, the investor made famous by The Big Short, talked about Oracle's new stock and bond sale:

"The market has become petrified of Oracle's balance sheet and its need for capital."

Microsoft just gave the market one more reason to be.

TIKR tracks 42 analysts on Oracle. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Oracle, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Oracle's Analyst Ratings

A small contract from a very big customer

The deal goes back to 2023, when Oracle agreed to give Microsoft access to servers for an AI-assisted version of Bing. Microsoft has reportedly been switching that capacity off in recent months. The servers run on older-generation chips that no longer meet its specifications. The deal's full size couldn't be determined, and Oracle says demand for its AI infrastructure is still strong, including for older GPUs.

Oracle has some evidence for that. On its first-quarter call in September, management said capacity up for renewal was renewed or resold at a 20% premium, even though most of those GPUs were four years old or older. So the chips Microsoft hands back should find another renter. My guess is that this contract is a rounding error next to Oracle's backlog (the Tencent deal was about 1% of it).

Splitting $300,000 evenly across Microsoft and IBM, plus Cisco, generates about $5,150 a year in dividends, a blended yield near 2%.

Microsoft yields under 1% but raised its quarterly dividend 8% and pays out only about 23% of earnings.

IBM pays the richest yield at roughly 3% and has paid dividends since 1916, though dividends eat 60% of free cash flow.

Plenty of retirees still think of tech stocks as growth plays that pay nothing while you wait. That view is out of date. Three of the biggest names in enterprise technology send cash to shareholders every quarter, and they have a long record of raising those payments.

raisbeckfoto / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images

A $300,000 investment, split into $100,000 in each of these three dividend payers, would produce about $5,150 in annual passive income, or more than $5,000 a year. That is modest for the money involved. This group appeals because the payout can grow fast, is well covered, and has reliably kept coming. Yields below are forward yields.

Microsoft Pays the Smallest Yield but Delivers the Fastest Raises

Stock #3: Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT)

Yield: 0.69%

Shares for $100,000: 176.02

Annual Passive Income: ~$690

Microsoft runs Azure, Microsoft 365, Windows, Xbox, and LinkedIn. Its yield is tiny because the stock has risen so far, giving it a market cap of about $4.02T. The dividend growth is where it stands out. The quarterly payout rose from $0.91 to $0.98, a 7.7% increase, and has risen every year since 2005 on the provided record.

Coverage is very strong. The $3.92 forward dividend works out to about 23% of fiscal 2026 EPS of $17.28. The main risk is spending: Microsoft expects calendar-year capex of approximately $170 billion, and free cash flow was $18.6 billion last quarter even though operating cash flow came in at $58 billion.
